newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, Australia urge greater economic ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, Australia urge greater economic ties.

text.p: Taiwan and Australia, which do not have diplomatic relations, on Thursday vowed to further strengthen bilateral economic and trade ties, despite earlier protests from China.

John Anderson, Canberra's minister for primary industries and energy, and executives from about 120 Australian firms arrived in Taiwan on Wednesday for a three-day business forum, the biggest held between the two sides.

"This event...is a graphic demonstration of the support and commitment by Australia to the Taiwan-Australia economic relationship and to its future development," Anderson told hundreds of officials and executives at the forum on Thursday.

China considers Taiwan a renegade province that is not entitled to international recognition. Beijing objects to contacts with Taipei by its diplomatic partners, and last month said it was "unacceptable" for Anderson to visit the island.
"We in Australia applaud Taiwan for its success in turning its economy into one of the most dynamic and competitive in the world," Anderson said.
Hundreds of individual meetings by businessmen from the two sides are expected to be held during the forum to seek further trade and investment opportunities.

"As Australia has developed high technology industry, we hope Australian companies will invest in Taiwan under our Asia Pacific Operation Centre project," said Chiang Ping-kun, head of Taiwan's Council for Economic Planning and Development.
Taipei unveiled the project in 1995, hoping to become a regional hub by attracting international companies to Taiwan.
"I encourage our Australian friends to come to promote your products here while Taiwan has the capacity to buy more from you," Chiang said.
The two sides are to discuss cooperation in agriculture, minerals, energy commodities, food, telecommunications and transport.
Taiwan is Australia's sixth largest export market, with exports totalling A$3.3 billion in 1995, according to Australia's trade office in Taipei.

Business contacts between Taiwan and Australia were boosted earlier this year when Taiwan's An Feng group signed a US$1.2 billion deal to build a slab mill in Australia with an annual production of 2.4 million tonnes.

In August, Australia said it was considering selling uranium to Taiwan, a move diplomats said risked straining already tense relations with Beijing. Chiang said Taiwan would consider buying uranium from any country if the purchase met international safety standards.
